messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
Need a hand. What would get me to about 19,000 feet?

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: The only stated goal is apogee about 19,000 ft. 19000 * 0.3048 = 5790 m, and "about" means stay within 5%, so the band is roughly 5500 to 6080 m. Motor, diameter, payload, and flight time are all free. Rail, wind, and landing speed are not given, so I assume a 1.5 m rail, 2 m/s wind, a vertical launch, and the usual 6 m/s touchdown limit. One stage unless the impulse budget forces a second.
2. Feasibility: With no drag, burnout speed for 5790 m is sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 5790) = 337 m/s. A real airframe throws away a large share of that energy to drag, so a mid-power motor will not get there. I want a K or an L, and I need real impulse and diameter numbers before I pick a tube.

2. Feasibility: The K550W is 1624.9 N*s in a 54 mm case and weighs 1.487 kg, but its only delay is 0 s, so it cannot coast. The L850W and L1150R are both about 3500 to 3700 N*s and 3.67 kg, and both are 75 mm cases. The Cesaroni 2765L730-P is 2763.2 N*s, 739.1 N average, 54 mm by 0.649 m, loaded mass 2.247 kg, and it has no ejection delay at all, so recovery has to be electronic. On a guessed 3.2 kg liftoff, 2763.2 / 3.2 = 864 m/s of ideal speed against the 337 m/s the altitude needs with no drag. That leaves a large budget for drag. The K is the same diameter with barely half the impulse, and the 75 mm motors buy impulse by getting fatter and heavier. The L730 is the one to try first.
3. Size: Liftoff mass guess 3.2 kg, motor included. Thrust-to-weight = 739.1 / (3.2 * 9.81) = 23.5. Rail acceleration (739.1 - 3.2 * 9.81) / 3.2 = 221 m/s^2, so exit speed sqrt(2 * 221 * 1.5) = 25.7 m/s, over the 15 m/s floor even before the thrust spike. Burnout mass is about 3.2 - 1.35 = 1.85 kg. A 5 m/s descent at Cd 0.8 needs 2 * 1.85 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 1.48 m^2, and sqrt(4 * 1.48 / 3.1416) = 1.37 m. A 1.5 m canopy sits a little under the 6 m/s limit. The case is 0.054 m, so a 1.2 mm phenolic wall makes the mount 0.054 + 2 * 0.0012 = 0.0564 m; I will use 0.057 m so the fit is not a knife edge. A 62 mm fiberglass tube, 0.062 m with a 1.6 mm wall, has room for that mount.
4. Draft: Ogive fiberglass nose 0.25 m on a 1.2 m fiberglass body, 0.062 m outside diameter, wall 0.0016 m. Phenolic mount 0.057 m by 0.66 m, wall 0.0012 m, 10 mm overhang, motor plugged. Three fiberglass fins, root 0.18 m, tip 0.08 m, span 0.1 m, sweep 0.09 m, 3 mm thick, set 0.01 m forward of the tail. A 0.04 kg altimeter and a 1.5 m ripstop chute deploy at apogee. Flying it on the default 1.5 m rail and 2 m/s wind.

4. Check: The simulator gives an apogee of 4471 m. Against 5790 m that is 4471 / 5790 = 0.772, and (5790 - 4471) / 5790 = 23% low, outside the 5% band. The rest passes: rail exit 31.6 m/s, thrust-to-weight 21.2, margin 2.22 cal through the burn, landing 5.0 m/s with the chute out at 23.5 s. Liftoff mass is 3.55 kg, about 11% over my 3.2 kg guess, and the warning flags supersonic body math at Mach 1.84. Mass alone does not explain a 23% miss; drag does.
5. Fix: Apogee is the failing value, 4471 m versus about 5790 m. A heavier coat of paint will not climb. I want more impulse in a 54 mm case so the 62 mm tube can stay. Looking up a longer L and an M before I redraw.

5. Fix: The 54 mm L1030 is only 2781.2 N*s, essentially the same impulse as the L730, so it will not climb. The L1355 is 4025 N*s but it is a 75 mm, 4.962 kg case. The M1297W is the useful step up: 5413.8 N*s, 1275 N average, 75 mm by 0.665 m, loaded mass 4.637 kg, and only a 0 s delay, so it stays plugged with an apogee chute. Impulse ratio 5413.8 / 2763.2 = 1.96. The old airframe was about 3.55 - 2.25 = 1.3 kg; a wider tube might make the new liftoff about 6.2 kg, and 6.2 / 3.55 = 1.75. Ideal speed goes from 2763.2 / 3.55 = 778 m/s to 5413.8 / 6.2 = 873 m/s, and (873 / 778)^2 = 1.26, so 4471 * 1.26 = 5630 m before the extra drag of the fatter tube. That is still short of 5790 m on paper, but close enough to fly. Thrust-to-weight 1275 / (6.2 * 9.81) = 21.0, and rail exit sqrt(2 * 196 * 1.5) = 24.2 m/s where (1275 - 6.2 * 9.81) / 6.2 = 196 m/s^2. The case is 0.075 m, so the mount goes to 0.079 m outside with a 1.5 mm wall, and the body and nose grow to 0.084 m with a 2 mm wall. Mount length 0.68 m still fits the 1.2 m tube. Fins and the 1.5 m chute stay put for this pass.

messages.content:
An AeroTech M1297W in an 84 mm fiberglass rocket, nose plus a 1.55 m tube, with a 2.0 m chute at apogee.
It leaves a 1.5 m rail at 26.7 m/s, holds 1.61 cal, and lands at 5.3 m/s.
Apogee is still 5160 m, about 11% under 19,000 ft, after three revisions. Smaller fins or more impulse would be the next move.
